newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's mutual fund sector seen set for growth.
newsitem.headline: Manila's mutual fund sector seen set for growth.

text.p: The Philippine mutual funds sector, fully recovered from a series of scandals in the 1960s, is growing rapidly in volume and reputation, industry officials said on Friday.
Assets of the country's six funds surged 70 percent in the past year, they said.

"This year, the assets level could nearly double again because at least three more funds are coming into the market," said Joby de Belen, marketing consultant at PhilEquity Fund, the country's most successful fund in terms of net asset value.
One of the entrants this year is the state-controlled pension fund, the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), which is planning to launch a one billion peso ($38 million) fund in March.

"The fund will be open to GSIS members and it will be a balanced fund investing in equities as well as fixed-income instruments like government securities," said Fernando Gaite, GSIS vice president for investment management.
GSIS, which runs a pension scheme for government employees, has assets of about 80 billion pesos.

Others planning to launch mutual funds this year include two brokerages, and they could be in the range of 500 million pesos each, said de Belen, who also runs a new magazine for Philippine mutual funds.

The country's six funds -- Philequity Fund, United Fund, Filipino Fund, First Galleon Fund, Citisec Fund, Philam Fund and Kabuhayan Fund -- together had net asset value of 2.424 billion pesos in 1996, up from 1.430 billion pesos a year earlier.
Philequity Fund reported a 194 percent increase in its investor base in 1996 and Philam Fund said its sales shot up 300 percent.
The growth comes on a very small base with Philequity now having only about 300 investors.
"But the economic situation is getting better, there are more players in the stock market and better acceptance of mutual funds, so the industry is bound to grow," said de Belen.
On the back of a growing economy, the Philippine Stock Exchange has boomed with market capitalisation surging in 1996 by 37 percent to 2,121 billion pesos from 1,545 billion pesos the previous year.
The boom helped the net asset values of aggressive funds, which put over 80 percent of their portfolio into equities.

So far this year, the stock market has notched up three new record closing highs and the euphoria from runaway profits is spreading the equity cult in a country originally wary of stock markets and mutual funds.
The country's first mutual funds were started in 1967.

"Unfortunately, there were one or two scams and that had a very negative effect," said Noel Gamo, corporate secretary of the Investment Company Association of the Philippines, which represents the country's mutual funds.

The funds folded because of a lack of regulation and allegations of mismanagement. They took hold again in the 1970s but the market collapsed after a revolt in the southern Philippines and the introduction of martial law.
Fund managers said the sector could get a further boost this year as the government is considering dropping a provision which at present imposes taxation on both the mutual fund and the investor.
